title: Orionid meteor shower offers overnight viewing in Thailand
excerpt: The best time to watch the Orionid meteor shower in Thailand is around 3am–5am on Thursday (October 22, 2026), provided skies are clear.
content:
The National Astronomical Research Institute of Thailand (NARIT) is inviting the public to watch the Orionid meteor shower on the night of Wednesday (October 21, 2026), continuing until dawn on Thursday (October 22, 2026).

The shower is expected to average about 20 meteors an hour at its peak, appearing in the eastern sky from around 10.30pm.

What causes the Orionid meteor shower?

The Orionids, also known as the “Orion meteor shower”, originate from the numerous dust particles and small fragments left behind by Halley’s Comet (1P/Halley).

As Earth crosses the comet’s orbital path, its gravity draws in this debris, which burns up through friction with the atmosphere.

The resulting flashes resemble fireballs radiating from the constellation Orion, giving the shower its name.

Although the meteors appear to emerge from that area, they can be seen anywhere in the sky.

When to watch the Orionids

According to NARIT, this year’s viewing period runs from the night of Wednesday (October 21, 2026), until dawn on Thursday (October 22, 2026), with the shower forecast to average about 20 meteors an hour at its peak.

The radiant, the point from which the meteors appear to originate, will be near the arm of the constellation Orion.

The radiant will appear in the east at around 10.30pm before gradually climbing towards the middle of the sky.

Observers can continue watching until dawn, although moonlight will interfere with viewing from early evening until about 2.30am.

The Thai Astronomical Society likewise puts the start of viewing at around 10.30pm, with the best opportunity in Thailand roughly between 3am and 5am on October 22, provided skies are clear and free of clouds.

However, bright moonlight this year may obscure fainter meteors, meaning observers could see fewer than the forecast peak rate, particularly in cities with extensive artificial lighting.
